the-five-remembrances.name: The five remembrances
the-five-remembrances.how: Each day, recollect slowly: I am subject to ageing; to illness; to death; I will be parted from all that is dear; I am the owner of my actions, and will inherit them. Let each one sink in before the next.
cautions: Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.

mindfulness-of-death-maranasati.name: Mindfulness of death (maranasati)
mindfulness-of-death-maranasati.how: At nightfall and daybreak, reflect that death could come tonight or today from many causes, and ask whether any unskilful quality is still unabandoned. Let the urgency feed effort, not fear.
cautions: Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.

recollecting-the-round.name: Recollecting the round
recollecting-the-round.how: Contemplate how long the round of birth and death has been, and how many losses it holds, until disenchantment with becoming arises. Then turn to the breath and rest.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.
Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.

powa-an-introduction-to-transference-at-.name: Powa: an introduction to transference at death
powa-an-introduction-to-transference-at-.how: Read a traditional introduction before seeking instruction from a qualified teacher: refuge, visualising Amitabha above the crown, and training the mind's direction at death. It is taught with empowerment, not from a page.

preparing-for-the-bardo.name: Preparing for the bardo
preparing-for-the-bardo.how: Notice the small gaps of daily life (falling asleep, the pause between thoughts) as rehearsals for the great transition, and rest there as awareness.
preparing-for-the-bardo.sourceLabel: Lion's Roar: The Fine Art of Conscious Dying (Glenn Mullin)
cautions: Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.

self-enquiry-who-dies.how: When the thought of death comes, ask to whom it comes. Trace the 'I' back to its source instead of following the thought. Ramana's own awakening began by lying down and enacting his death.

practising-dying-melete-thanatou.name: Practising dying (melete thanatou)
practising-dying-melete-thanatou.how: Socrates calls philosophy the practice of dying: loosening the soul's grip on the body's pleasures and fears, day by day. Read the Phaedo slowly as an exercise, not an argument.
cautions: Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.

analytic-meditation-on-the-stages-of-the.name: Analytic meditation on the stages of the path
analytic-meditation-on-the-stages-of-the.how: Pick one Lamrim topic, such as the preciousness of this human life or the certainty of death. Think it through step by step, using reasons and examples, until a felt conviction comes. Then rest single-pointedly on that conviction for a while. Alternate thinking and resting.
cautions: Reflections on death can stir grief. Go gently, and set the practice aside if it overwhelms you.

self-enquiry.name: Self-enquiry
self-enquiry.how: Whenever a thought arises, ask to whom it arises; the answer is 'to me'; then ask 'who am I?' and hold attention on the sense of I.

contemplating-not-self.name: Contemplating not-self
contemplating-not-self.how: Take each aggregate in turn and ask: is it constant, is it easeful, is it fitting to regard it as me, mine, my self?

shiva-process-self-inquiry.name: Shiva Process self-inquiry
shiva-process-self-inquiry.how: Bring to mind a situation that is troubling you. Describe what you feel in plain words, then ask "what is the deeper feeling under this?" and keep going, layer by layer, until something shifts and the contraction releases. Often done in pairs or with a guide.

what-am-i-don-t-know.name: "What am I? Don't know"
what-am-i-don-t-know.how: Ask "What am I?" deeply on the in-breath. On the out-breath, hold "Don't know..." as long as the breath lasts. Return to this don't-know mind in every activity, and keep clear about the next correct action. This is Seung Sahn's Kwan Um teaching.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

owner-of-my-actions.how: The fifth remembrance: I am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions. Recollect it before acting and after.

mindfulness-of-breathing.name: Mindfulness of breathing
mindfulness-of-breathing.how: Sit comfortably, know the in-breath and out-breath, then let the breath calm the whole body before turning to feelings and mind.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

goodwill-metta.name: Goodwill (metta)
goodwill-metta.how: Wish yourself well, then widen the wish to others, near and far, seen and unseen, without exception.

resting-in-the-gap-between-breaths-vijna.name: Resting in the gap between breaths (Vijñāna Bhairava dhāraṇā)
resting-in-the-gap-between-breaths-vijna.how: Sit comfortably and breathe naturally. Notice the instant where the in-breath turns into the out-breath, and the instant where the out-breath turns back. Do not hold the breath; simply let attention fall into each turning point and rest there for its brief duration. Over time, notice the open awareness that is present in the pause.

recognition-pratyabhijna-contemplation.name: Recognition (pratyabhijñā) contemplation
recognition-pratyabhijna-contemplation.how: Read one sūtra of the Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam slowly. Then look at present experience — a sound, a thought, a feeling — and ask whether anything appears outside awareness. Let the understanding "this too is a form of the one consciousness" settle as a felt recognition rather than an idea. Return to the text, then to experience, alternating.
recognition-pratyabhijna-contemplation.sourceLabel: Christopher Wallis on the twenty sūtras of the Pratyabhijñāhṛdayam.

drawing-the-sri-chakra-as-meditation.name: Drawing the Śrī Chakra as meditation
drawing-the-sri-chakra-as-meditation.how: Following a teacher's step-by-step construction, draw the Śrī Yantra slowly from the centre point (bindu) outward: the nine interlocking triangles, the lotus rings and the square gateways. Treat each stage as a contemplation of the goddess unfolding into the world, not as geometry homework.
drawing-the-sri-chakra-as-meditation.sourceLabel: Devipuram, "How to Draw Sri Chakra" parts 1–2.

basic-saiva-siddhanta-meditation.name: Basic Śaiva Siddhānta meditation
basic-saiva-siddhanta-meditation.how: Sit upright, regulate the breath to a slow even count, then draw awareness inward from the senses to the spine and to the inner light, holding a single point of focus. Hinduism Today's monastery teaches it as part of daily worship and study.
basic-saiva-siddhanta-meditation.sourceLabel: Bodhinatha Veylanswami, "How Do We Meditate? Part 1".
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

mantra-repetition-japa.name: Mantra repetition (japa)
mantra-repetition-japa.how: Choose a mantra received from your tradition, sit with a mala, and repeat it at an even pace, aloud, whispered or mentally. Let attention rest on the sound and its meaning; when the mind wanders, return to the next repetition.

anapanasati-breath-meditation-method-2.name: Ānāpānasati (breath meditation, "Method 2")
anapanasati-breath-meditation-method-2.tradLabel: Dhammayut forest line (Ajahn Mun → Maha Boowa / Ajaan Lee)
anapanasati-breath-meditation-method-2.how: Sit upright and notice the breath at whatever point it is clearest. Let it settle into a comfortable rhythm, then let that sense of ease spread through the whole body, using the breath energy as a home base for steady, alert attention.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

buddho-recollection.name: "Buddho" recollection
buddho-recollection.how: Silently repeat "bud-" on the in-breath and "-dho" on the out-breath to anchor the mind; when the mind is calm, drop the word and stay with the knowing itself. Used widely in the Ajahn Mun and Ajahn Chah lines.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

walking-meditation-jongrom.tradLabel: Ajahn Chah line (Wat Nong Pah Pong)
walking-meditation-jongrom.how: Choose a straight path of 15–30 paces. Walk at a natural or slow pace, attention on the feet or the whole body; at each end, stop, turn, and re-collect before walking back.

mahasi-noting.name: Mahasi noting
mahasi-noting.how: Watch the rise and fall of the abdomen and give each event a soft mental label ("rising", "falling", "thinking", "hearing"), then return to the primary object; move to slow walking with labels for lifting, moving and placing.

natural-awareness-right-attitude.name: Natural awareness (right attitude)
natural-awareness-right-attitude.how: Instead of forcing focus on one object, relax and know whatever is being experienced, checking the attitude of the observing mind (craving, aversion, impatience) throughout daily activities.

satipatthana-four-establishings-of-mindf.name: Satipaṭṭhāna (four establishings of mindfulness)
satipatthana-four-establishings-of-mindf.how: Contemplate body, feeling, mind and mental qualities as they arise and pass, ardent, clearly knowing and mindful, without greed or distress about the world (MN 10).

rain.name: RAIN
rain.how: Recognise what is happening; Allow it to be there; Investigate with kindness how it feels in the body; Nurture with self-compassion; then rest in the awareness that remains.

open-awareness-shamatha-without-a-suppor.name: Open awareness (shamatha without a support)
open-awareness-shamatha-without-a-suppor.how: After a few minutes with a support, let it go. Leave the eyes open and the gaze soft. Let sights, sounds and thoughts come and go, and do not follow them or push them away. When you get caught up, simply notice it and relax again. The point is to rest as the knowing that is already present.

looking-at-the-mind-mahamudra.name: Looking at the mind (Mahamudra)
looking-at-the-mind-mahamudra.how: Once the mind is calm, turn and look for the one who is looking. Ask where a thought comes from, where it stays, and where it goes. Do not reason about it; just look and rest in whatever is seen or not found. This practice is traditionally done under a qualified teacher's guidance.

resting-in-rigpa-dzogchen-orientation-on.name: Resting in rigpa (Dzogchen), orientation only
resting-in-rigpa-dzogchen-orientation-on.how: In Dzogchen, the student is introduced to the nature of mind (rigpa) by a teacher. Between sessions, practitioners recall that recognition, leave it uncontrived for short moments, many times, and release any effort to improve it. This entry describes the practice and is not a substitute for the introduction itself.
cautions: Orientation only: this practice is traditionally learned from a qualified teacher in its lineage. Read and listen; do not attempt it from a summary.

shikantaza-just-sitting.name: Shikantaza (just sitting)
shikantaza-just-sitting.how: Sit as in zazen, but drop counting and any object. Simply sit, aware of the whole posture and the whole field of experience, without chasing or suppressing anything. When you find yourself lost in thought, come back to the posture. Dogen treats the sitting itself as realisation, not as a means to it.

koan-practice-with-mu.name: Koan practice with Mu
koan-practice-with-mu.how: Take up "Does a dog have buddha nature? Mu" (Zhaozhou). Breathe Mu on each exhalation and put your whole doubt into it. Do not interpret it. Present your understanding to a teacher in private interview (dokusan). Koan work depends on that meeting with a teacher.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

silent-illumination-mozhao.how: Relax the body and be aware of the whole body sitting. Widen that awareness to include the environment, without any centre or edge. Silence means not adding commentary; illumination means remaining clearly aware. Rest there, and return whenever you get caught.

bhairavi-sadhana-isha.name: Bhairavi Sadhana (Isha)
bhairavi-sadhana-isha.how: A lay devotional observance offered by the Isha Foundation around Linga Bhairavi: for a set period the practitioner keeps simple disciplines (as given by Isha), offers daily devotion to the goddess, and completes it with an offering at a Linga Bhairavi abode. sravanamanananididhyasana.name: Śravaṇa–manana–nididhyāsana
sravanamanananididhyasana.how: Systematic listening to the Upaniṣads with a teacher (śravaṇa), resolving doubts by reflection (manana), and dwelling on the understood meaning until it is assimilated (nididhyāsana).

japa-repetition-of-a-divine-name.name: Japa (repetition of a divine name)
japa-repetition-of-a-divine-name.how: Repeat a mantra or name of God given by the teacher, often with a mālā of 108 beads, letting the mind rest in its meaning and the feeling of devotion.

hare-krishna-mahamantra-japa-and-kirtan.how: Chant "Hare Kṛṣṇa Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa Hare Hare / Hare Rāma Hare Rāma, Rāma Rāma Hare Hare" softly on beads (japa) or sing it together (kīrtan), as practised since Chaitanya.

nembutsu-nianfo.name: Nembutsu / nianfo
nembutsu-nianfo.how: Recite "Namu Amida Butsu" (Japanese) or "Namo Amituofo" (Chinese), aloud or silently, with a mala if you like. In Chinese Pure Land, recitation is a practice of concentration and aspiration for rebirth. In Shin Buddhism, it is an expression of gratitude for Amida's vow, not a means of earning anything.

christian-meditation-with-a-mantra-maran.name: Christian meditation with a mantra (Maranatha)
christian-meditation-with-a-mantra-maran.how: Sit still and upright with your eyes lightly closed. Silently repeat one prayer-word, "Ma-ra-na-tha", in four equal syllables, listening to it rather than thinking about its meaning. When thoughts or images arrive, return to the word, without force. Sit for 20–30 minutes, morning and evening.

centering-prayer.name: Centering Prayer
centering-prayer.how: Choose a sacred word as a sign of consent to God's presence. Sit comfortably and bring it in gently. When you notice you are engaged with a thought, return ever so gently to the word. End by resting in silence for a couple of minutes. Twice daily, 20 minutes.

lectio-divina.how: Read a short scripture passage slowly, then again; notice the word that catches you; respond to it in prayer; rest in silence. Read, ponder, pray, rest.

zikr-remembrance-in-the-inayati-way.how: Sitting quietly, repeat the phrase of divine unity (La ilaha illa'llah) aloud or silently, letting the breath and a gentle movement of the head carry it, until the remembrance continues on its own in the heart.

weekly-parashah-reflection-neo-hasidic.how: Each week read the Torah portion with a Hasidic commentary in mind and look for the inward, devotional teaching it holds for this week of your life.

calming-and-contemplation-zhiguan.name: Calming and contemplation (zhiguan)
calming-and-contemplation-zhiguan.how: First calm the mind (zhi) by settling the breath and posture. Then contemplate (guan) any present thought as simultaneously empty, provisionally existing, and the middle, which are the threefold truth. Zhiyi's Mohe zhiguan sets out four kinds of samadhi practice (constant sitting, constant walking, half-walking half-sitting, and neither).
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

rudi-s-double-breath.name: Rudi's double breath
rudi-s-double-breath.how: Breathe in, bringing attention down from the throat into the heart, and then down to the navel and the base of the body. Breathing out, let the energy rise up the spine. Keep the movement gentle and continuous, and return to the heart when attention scatters.

khecari-mudra-historical-description-onl.name: Khecarī mudrā (historical description only)
khecari-mudra-historical-description-onl.how: Described in haṭha texts as turning the tongue back and up into the cavity above the soft palate, sometimes after gradually lengthening the tongue. dream-yoga-first-steps.name: Dream yoga, first steps
dream-yoga-first-steps.how: During the day, keep reminding yourself "this is a dream" so that the habit carries into sleep. Before sleep, set a strong intention to recognise dreams. Visualise a luminous syllable at the throat as you fall asleep. Each morning, review whether you recognised a dream, and renew the intention.

feeding-your-demons-a-modern-adaptation-.name: Feeding your demons (a modern adaptation of Chöd)

Rest in the open space that remains.

shamatha-with-object.name: Calm abiding with a support
shamatha-with-object.how: Sit upright and relaxed. Rest your attention lightly on a simple support, such as the breath at the nostrils, a pebble, or a sound. When you notice the mind has wandered, return to the support without scolding yourself. Aim for many short, clear sessions rather than a few long, dull ones. Over time, loosen your grip until attention rests on its own.

tonglen.name: Tonglen (sending and taking)
tonglen.how: Flash briefly on open, spacious mind. Then breathe in a feeling of heaviness and heat, and breathe out a feeling of coolness and light. Start with a real person who is suffering, perhaps yourself, and breathe in their pain while breathing out relief. Widen this to everyone who feels the same. Keep it simple and close to how you actually feel.

nine-breathings.name: Nine breathings of purification
nine-breathings.how: Visualise the three channels: a central blue channel with a white one on the right and a red one on the left. Breathe in through the right nostril and out through the left three times, releasing anger. Then breathe in through the left and out through the right three times, releasing attachment. Finally, breathe in through both and push the breath up the central channel three times, releasing ignorance. Rest afterwards.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

zazen.name: Zazen posture and breath
zazen.how: Sit on a cushion with your knees on the floor, or on a chair, with the spine upright. Rest the hands in the cosmic mudra, left on right with the thumbs lightly touching, and keep the eyes half-open and lowered. Breathe naturally through the nose. Beginners can count breaths from one to ten and start again whenever they lose count.
cautions: Keep the breath natural and unforced. Stop if you feel dizzy, anxious or unwell.

huatou.how: Take up a short question, such as "What is wu?" or "Before my parents were born, what was my original face?" walking-meditation.how: Walk slowly and coordinate your steps with your breath, for example two steps on the in-breath and three on the out-breath. Feel each foot touching the earth as if kissing it. You are not trying to arrive anywhere; every step is the arrival.

ajikan.how: Shingon practitioners visualise the Sanskrit syllable A on a moon disc above a lotus. The A signifies the unborn source of all things. They join it with the breath and expand the moon until it fills the universe, then contract it into the heart. Formal ajikan is taught after initiation; this entry is an orientation only.

middle-pillar-outline.name: The Middle Pillar (outline)
middle-pillar-outline.tradLabel: Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn
middle-pillar-outline.how: Stand or sit straight. Picture a slender pillar of light along the midline of the body. Bring attention to five centers in turn, seeing each as a sphere of its colour: brilliant white above the crown; soft lavender at the throat; rose pink at the heart; deep violet at the loins; and at the feet the four earth tones quartered. Dwell briefly at each. Then picture light circulating: down the front of the body and up the spine, around and around, steady with the breath. Close by letting the light settle and fade. Learn the full form from the order or a qualified teacher; this outline only shows what the exercise is.

vbt-sound-dissolution.name: Listening to the inner sound (VBT verses 38-39)
vbt-sound-dissolution.how: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle by itself. Listen for a faint inner sound, a soft ringing or hum beneath the sounds of the room. Rest attention on it lightly, without straining to hear. Let it be loud, soft, present or absent; do not follow it into images or stories. When the mind wanders, come back to listening. If the sound fades into quiet, rest in the quiet. When you finish, notice the ordinary sounds around you again.

recollection-of-past-lives-orientation.name: Recollection of former lives (pubbenivāsānussati): orientation
recollection-of-past-lives-orientation.how: In the early discourses this is the first of the three knowledges the Buddha describes on the night of his awakening (MN 4). The later manual, Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga (chapter XIII), presents it as a by-product of fully mastered concentration: only after the fourth jhāna is steady does a meditator turn the mind back, sitting by sitting, through the day, childhood and birth, and, the texts say, beyond. Both sources treat it as a side-effect of a calm, purified mind and as fuel for disenchantment with the round of birth and death, never as a goal or a sign of progress. Satsang gives orientation only. The groundwork anyone can do is the breath meditation and the reflection on the round in this course; the knowledge itself is traditionally developed under a teacher inside a long retreat.
recollection-of-past-lives-orientation.sourceLabel: MN 4 (dhammatalks.org); Visuddhimagga XIII, tr. Ñāṇamoli, The Path of Purification (Access to Insight). Satsang summary in its own words.
cautions: No results are promised. Memories that seem to surface in meditation can be imagination or old impressions; the tradition warns against clinging to them either way.

collections.intro: Seven days of foundation for Abhinavagupta and VBT study: steady breath, the turn of the breath, and recognition. Ten minutes a day. Initiated practices are not here: when the gap is steady, take the next step with a qualified teacher in the tradition.

units.title: Settle
units.intro: The home base: ease through the body with the breath.

items.note: Where is the breath clearest today? That is your seat for the week.

units.title: The turn
units.intro: Notice where the in-breath becomes the out-breath. Rest there; hold nothing.

items.note: Did you find the turning, or the idea of it? Either is fine — noted, not judged.

units.title: Recognition
units.intro: One sutra slowly, then look: does anything appear outside awareness?

items.note: Write one sentence on what recognition felt like versus what you thought about it.

units.title: Return to ease
units.intro: Same foundation, deeper seat. The gap work needs a rested body.

items.note: Compare today with day 1: steadier, sleepier, brighter? Log it plainly.

units.title: Longer turn
units.intro: Same gap practice, full sit. Let attention fall in; never force it.

items.note: If strain appears, drop back to ease. The gap is found, not made.

units.title: Recognition again
units.intro: Same contemplation, fresh experience. Sound, thought, feeling — inside or outside?

items.note: One line for the journal: what was recognised, and by what?

units.title: The week in one sit
units.intro: Ease, then the turn, then recognition — one short sit chaining all three in order.

items.note: Which of the three is your door? That is what you take to a teacher next.

collections.title: VBT Foundations
collections.author: Wiser
collections.intro: Seven contemplative practices from the Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra, in a progression from the breath to daily life (not the text's own order): the turn of the breath, the gap between objects, inner sound, the body as awareness, the sense spaces, spaciousness, and the end-of-twelve through the day. Each is a quiet sit you can do on your own. The rest of the text (breath retention, mantra, the subtle-body practices) is learned from a qualified teacher: when one of these becomes your door, take it to a teacher in the tradition.

units.title: Breath-pause
units.intro: The first practice the text presents: resting in the gap between the in-breath and the out-breath.

items.note: Did you find the turning, or the idea of it? Either is fine — noted, not judged.

units.title: The gap between thoughts
units.intro: When the mind lets go of one thing and before it takes up the next, rest in the middle. Build on day 1's steadiness.

items.note: How long was the gap today? One thought-width, or longer?

units.title: Inner sound
units.intro: Listen to the subtle inner sound until sound dissolves into silence.

items.note: What quality was the sound — ring, hum, tone, silence? Log it plainly.

units.title: Body as consciousness
units.intro: Conceive of the body — or the whole universe — as nothing but consciousness. A felt sense, not an idea.

items.note: Did the body-sense shift, or was it the same body with a different label? Both are data.

units.title: Inner and outer spaces
units.intro: A sense contact — the outer space where it arrives, the inner space where it is received, both as one field.

items.note: Which side did attention collapse into — inner or outer? That is the habit to notice.

units.title: Spaciousness
units.intro: The space of the room, the space inside the body, the skin as a thin wall between: one open field.

items.note: When did the mind grasp for something solid? What did it grasp at?

units.title: The end-of-twelve through the day
units.intro: Not a sitting practice. A few times today, let attention touch the space just above the crown for a breath or two, then carry on.

items.note: How many times today did you remember? The remembering is the practice, not the count.
